Priya S: Headline — ACME customer on Dedicated seeing intermittent 429s and a couple of 401s during a bulk ingest. Started after they bumped context to ~64k and turned on streaming. They also reported a billing mismatch (charged for tokens but got 401 on retry). Need repro steps + root cause.
Ben T: Ok can you paste a raw request/headers and any x-rate-limit-* headers from responses? Also which model variant and region?
Priya S: Model=redwood-extended-64k (dedicated pool rwd-prod-us-east-2). Example response headers from them:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Date: Mon, 09 Jan 2026 12:10:22 GMT
X-Req-Id: 7f3a2d
X-RateLimit-Limit-RPM: 60
X-RateLimit-Remaining-RPM: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 13
X-Model-Concurrency-Limit: 4
Content-Type: application/json

Body: {"error":"rate limit exceeded","code":429}
Priya S: And then later they got a 401 on a retry:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Date: Mon, 09 Jan 2026 12:11:05 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Body: {"error":"invalid auth token"}
Ben T: Hmm 429 then 401 — could be a race where their token rotation failed while we rate-limited the retry attempts. Did they use a signing proxy or short-lived keys?
Priya S: They rotate every 5m via an internal proxy (customer-managed). They claim the proxy logs show successful signing; token looks fine. But billing note: tokens were charged for the initial call even though it 429'd. Customer upset.
Mona L: Quick notes from runtime side: 1) For long-context models we enforce both RPM/TPM and per-model concurrency. 2) Long-context request cost counting happens at request acceptance time: tokens consumed may be registered even if the request later receives 429 during serving (e.g., enqueued then dropped). This can look like "charged but failed". 3) We also have a separate long-context throttling heuristic to prevent OOMs: if KV cache pressure + concurrent long requests > threshold we start rejecting with 429s and set a tighter per-model concurrency for that pool.
Shreyas R: To add: our Dedicated pools have a soft burst window (short-term borrow) and a hard per-model RPM/TPM enforced by the control plane. If many clients fan out retries quickly it quickly exhausts the short borrow, causing 429s with remaining=0. Also note streaming changes: streaming opens a steady connection that still counts toward concurrency while chunks are processed.
Ben T: Useful. Priya — can you ask the customer for a minimal repro script that does the following: 1) single-threaded loop send same payload with 64k context, 2) include their proxy auth header, 3) capture full response headers and body. If they can't reproduce reliably, we can run a controlled repro from our staging dedicated pool.
Priya S: I have a snippet they ran. sharing:```bash
# naive repro: send 100 requests sequentially
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -D - \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROXY_TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"redwood-extended-64k","input":"'"$(yes X | head -c 65000)"'"}' \
    https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate >> /tmp/repro-$i.log
  sleep 0.5
done
```Priya S: They said when they remove streaming and push as non-streaming requests, failures drop significantly.
Mona L: That matches expectation: streaming holds the connection and concurrency slot longer. For long context, time-in-flight per request increases, so effective concurrency is higher even if RPM is low. Two levers: reduce parallelism/retries, or use the non-streaming endpoint which lets the runtime schedule work more compactly.
Ben T: For the billing/charged issue — please open a billing ticket with billing-team and include original request-id (X-Req-Id) and timestamps. We can evaluate crediting if ingestion was dropped after enqueuing. But explain to customer that token accounting sometimes occurs early.
Priya S: Understood. Customer also wants permanent fix — they asked if we can increase their concurrency for the dedicated pool.
Shreyas R: We can raise per-customer concurrency but it's gated by pool capacity. Options: 1) increase reserved capacity on their Dedicated contract (recommended), 2) enable controlled canary for higher concurrency during off-peak, 3) change routing policy to route long-context to machines with more mem per instance (if available).
Mona L: Quick troubleshooting checklist I recommend we run now:
- Repro on staging with their exact payload + streaming toggled on/off
- Replay their token rotation to verify 401 timing (collect proxy logs)
- Collect control-plane rate-limit event log for that customer around the timestamp (we can pull from internal rate_limit_events index)
- Check pool-level KV cache memory pressure metrics and queue length around 12:09-12:12

Ben T: I'll pull their rate_limit_events and attach here when done. Priya, can you also ask them to send a single failing request curl with -v output (so we can see TLS and full headers)?
Priya S: Yep asking now. Also they reported "x-rate-limit-reset: 13" which suggests a short window — is that seconds?
Mona L: reset value is in seconds until window reset (we use sliding windows for RPM/TPM). 13 seconds means they should see allowance after that. But if they retry aggressively before reset or have multiple simultaneous clients, it'll still 429.
ops-bot: [alert] dedicated-prod-us-east-2: pool queue length spike detected (12:09:48) — current queue 38, threshold 30 — notifying eng-runtime
Ben T: I pulled the event log snippet:
{"ts":1924123462,"cust":"acct-ACME","model":"redwood-extended-64k","event":"rate_limit_exceeded","type":"rpm","limit":60,"remaining":0}
Ben T: Also found a cluster-side auth error at 12:11:04 matching the customer's 401 — looks like proxy sent an expired token then refreshed, but the retry landed while our auth cache still had stale mapping; we have a bug where short-lived proxy tokens + concurrent retries can cause transient 401 surface. I've filed a follow-up with eng-auth.
Mona L: Action items for eng-runtime: 1) instrument an acceptance-phase vs serving-phase token accounting flag so billing can differentiate charged-but-never-served; 2) verify we enforce a separate long-context concurrency soft cap earlier in the admission path so customers get deterministic 429s (we'll tune thresholds); 3) ensure rate-limit headers emitted include more explicit bucket names (rpm/tpm/concurrency) to aid debugging.
Shreyas R: For immediate mitigation: advise customer to (a) reduce client-side parallelism and add jitter on retries, (b) use non-streaming for heavy context, (c) consider smaller chunks or pre-embedding to reduce token size.
Priya S: I'll pass this to the customer with repro steps and ask for their curl -v. Also initiating billing ticket. Thanks all — will update when I have curl -v and their proxy logs.
Mona L: FYI, we'll spin a small controlled repro in staging with similar pool settings and share results. Expect a follow-up in ~2-4h.
Priya S: Great — marking follow-up ETA 4h. :thumbsup:
